title: Simulating Data
content:
The examples we've been working with have mostly been about analyzing existing data. We tend to follow a similar pattern each time:

1.  Read data in from a file
2.  Look for some characteristics/process the data
3.  Plot the data to see trends, patterns, extremes, etc.

MATLAB is also widely used to **simulate data**. When we simulate data, we also tend to follow a similar pattern each time:

1.  Convert the math equations into a computer program
2.  Create a starter set of data and use the computer program from step 1 to generate predicted data
3.  Look for some things / process data / plot data to see trends, etc.

Math equations tend to look something like this:

$$y=sin(x)$$

We know that this equation is really saying: $y$ is equal to the sine of $x$ for all possible values of $x$, no matter how big or small or precise those numbers are. You might be able to type

$$plot(sin)$$

into a graphing calculator and get a plot containing a sine wave because the graphing calculator knows that you probably mean: show me a plot of the values of the sine of $x$ vs. $x$ for all possible values of $x$, no matter how big or small or precise those numbers are. But if we type

$$plot(sin)$$

into MATLAB, we get an error message because MATLAB doesn't know that we mean `sin` to really mean $sin(x)$ and $x$ to be a variable with all possible values of $x$. So MATLAB says, _"¯ \\ _(ツ)_ /¯ lol whatever"_ and gives us an error message.

To run a simulation in MATLAB, we first need to create a _starter set of data_. In Homework 2, we created vectors and matrices, and we saw that range notation ( `start:step:last` ) was quite convenient for creating a starter set of data. In our earlier attempt to plot $sin(x)$, we noted that the plot function requires a set of ordered pairs, e.g. $(x\_1,y\_1)$, $(x\_2,y\_2)$, $(x\_3,y\_3)$, etc. We can generate these easily using vectorized code!

title: Variance and Standard Deviation
content:
The mean, median, and mode of a dataset are useful starting points for understanding the characteristics of a dataset, but they are single numbers that describe the average, middle, and most common values (the central tendencies) of the dataset.

**Variance** and **standard deviation** are measures that tell us how "spread out" a dataset is. The standard deviation is just the square root of the variance.

Here is a histogram (or **distribution** ) of data that is more _narrow_ - more of the data points are grouped around a central value (0 in this case):

Here is a histogram of data that is more _wide_ - more of the data points are farther away from a central value (0 in this case):

The more narrow distribution's variance is smaller than the wider distribution's variance. Similarly, the more narrow distribution's standard deviation is smaller than the wider distribution's standard deviation. _Therefore, the smaller the variance (or standard deviation), the more narrow the distribution will be._

Important things to note when we compare these two figures:

*   The x-axes have the same limits, and the y-axes have the same limits. This allows us to directly compare the data visually.
*   These figures also have the same underlying "type" of data (normally-distributed random numbers), allowing us to directly compare the variance and standard deviation when we state, "This variance is smaller than that variance." (Comparing the variance of the height of a blade of grass to the variance of the top speed of cheetahs makes no sense.)
*   Variance and standard deviation only offer an aggregate measure of the spread of a dataset. It's often important to consider the shape of the distribution as well (e.g. is it a bell curve or a uniform distribution?).

MATLAB has built-in functions to calculate the variance and standard deviation:

*   `var` - variance
*   `std` - standard deviation

These functions work similarly to all the other built-in functions that calculate statistical measures of a data set (e.g. `max`, `mean`, etc.)

**Warning!**

If you want to take the variance (or standard deviation) of all elements in a matrix `M`, don't use `var(var(M))` - that's not correct because the variance of the column variances is not mathematically equivalent to the variance of the whole dataset. Instead, use either of the other approaches, `var(M(:))` or `var(M, 0, 'all')` (the `0` is a weighting value; you can look up the `var` function in the MATLAB documentation to learn more).

title: Projectile Motion
content:
Let's practice simulating a process in MATLAB.

**Projectile motion** is a well-known process: you see projectile motion anytime you throw something through the air:

In the real world, there are a lot of things going on when you throw an item through the air:

*   the initial speed you give to the item
*   the angle that you throw it at relative to the ground
*   drag
*   lift
*   gravity
*   cross winds
*   lots more things!

Wow, that _is_ a lot! Too much for what we want to practice with today, so we'll make some assumptions:

1.  We assume that only gravity is acting on this item; we will neglect drag, lift, cross-winds, ill-timed flying insects, etc.
    
2.  We assume that we are all excellent throwers, and we can throw an item with exactly the stated initial speed, $v\_0$, and initial angle to the ground, $θ$.
    

Given these assumptions, our thrown item's position over time is given by these equations:

$$\\begin{aligned}x &=v\_0 \\cos(\\theta) t \\\\y &=v\_0 \\sin(\\theta) t - \\frac{1}{2} g t^2\\end{aligned}$$

where $t$ is time, $x$ is the horizontal distance at time $t$, $y$ is the vertical distance at time $t$, $v\_0$ is the initial speed of the item at time $t=0$, $\\theta$ is the initial angle of the item at time $t=0$, and $g$ is the gravitational acceleration (we will assume $g=9.8$ m/s$^2$).

These are well-established equations governing this simplified projectile motion, but MATLAB can't understand these equations -- these are math equations! Before we can simulate our item's projectile motion, we need to translate these math equations into statements that MATLAB can execute:

x \= v0 .\* cos(theta) .\* t
y \= v0 .\* sin(theta) .\* t \- 9.8 .\* t.^2 ./ 2

In these statements, `t` is a vector representing time values (with units of seconds), `x` is a vector representing horizontal distance (in meters) based on the values in the vector `t`, `y` is a vector representing vertical distance (in meters) based on the values in the vector `t`, `v0` is the initial speed (in m/s) of the item at time $t=0$, `theta` is the initial angle (in radians) of the item at time $t=0$, and the $g$ was replaced with `9.8` since we assume that the gravitational acceleration is constant and is in m/s$^2$.

We can simulate the $(x,y)$ position of the item as a function of time once we **create a starter set of time values for `t`** . A starter set of data like we need here typically consists of equally spaced numbers created using either `linspace` or range notation.

  

##### Exercise 1

You have thrown an item. Create a new MATLAB script called `ProjectileMotion.m` to calculate the item's $(x,y)$ position for an **initial speed of 40 m/s** and an **initial angle of pi/4 radians (45 degrees)** over the course of **15 seconds**.

Follow this algorithm for the `ProjectileMotion.m` script:

1.  Create variables for the initial conditions ( `v0` and `theta` ) and give them the values for this simulation.
    
2.  Create a "starter set" of data for `t` consisting of equally spaced numbers using either `linspace` or range notation.

title: Debug Sum-of-Products circuit (waveform only)
content:
Example Bug Finding Using Waveform Viewer

##### Example: Finding a semantic bug using a waveform viewer

module buggy(out, in1, in2);
  // Port and wire declarations
  output out;
  input  in1, in2;
  wire   w1, w2, w3;

  // Gates
  and a1(w1, in1, in2);
  and a2(w3, in1, w2);
  or  o1(out, w1, w3);
endmodule

Suppose you created an exhaustive test bench for the module above. You could potentially see a terminal output like the following.

coder@d5b148ae0d6c:~/workspace$ iverilog \-Wall \-o buggy buggy.v buggy\_tb.v
coder@d5b148ae0d6c:~/workspace$ ./buggy
VCD info: dumpfile test.vcd opened for output.
inputs \= in  outputs \= out
in1 \= 0 in2 \= 0   outputs \= 0   time \=  0
in1 \= 0 in2 \= 1   outputs \= 0   time \= 10
in1 \= 1 in2 \= 0   outputs \= x   time \= 20
in1 \= 1 in2 \= 1   outputs \= 1   time \= 30
coder@d5b148ae0d6c:~/workspace$ 

There were no syntax errors, but buggy has an error if we were not expecting the `x` for `in==1` `in2==0`. To find the error, one tactic you could use is to open the waveform viewer by clicking on the `test.vcd` file (might need to click on it twice or three times). You would see something like the following.

To get a peek into what is happening inside your module, click on the big blue "Add Signals" button.

This pulls up a list of the signals in your test bench. The first signal `out` is a wire in your test bench. The second two signals ( `in1` and `in2` ) are the `reg` signals in your test bench that you assigned in your testbench. These first three signals are what your testbench passed to/from the instance of the `buggy` circuit.

The remaining signals all have the word `bug` in front of them. `bug` is the name of the circuit instance we gave our buggy circuit (e.g., `buggy bug(out, in1, in2);` ) in our test bench (This is why module names are important!). In this set of signals, you also see the wires `w1`, `w2`, and `w3` that we declared inside the `buggy` module. Note: if we had a second buggy module instance called `insect`, we would see another set of signals called `insect in1`, `insect in2`, etc.,

We recommend working backward from your output to see if you can isolate where your error is coming from. Since output is determined by `w1` and `w3`, let's add those wires and `out` to our waveform. With some zooming in, you might see the following.

From this screenshot, we see that `w3` is the likely source of the bug because it has value `x`. We would then want to add the signals that determine the value of `w3` : `in1` and `w2`.

From this screenshot, we see that `w2` was never properly assigned a value, so it is the source of the semantic bug. You would want to look through your code and verify that `w2` is never the output of a module or is never assigned a value. You would then need to think about the expected behavior of your circuit and decide what to do about `w2`.

##### Alternate Example

Let's consider one more example. Suppose you had slightly different code from the original example and opened `test.vcd` and added the signals like last time and saw the following instead.

In this example, `in1` and `w2` are not the source of the `x` output for `w3` since both signals are never `x` or `z`. In this case, `w3` is probably `x` because another gate is also trying to assign to `w3`. In this case, you would want to look through your code to find two modules that both have output `w3` or two `assign` statements that assign to `w3`.

Waveform Viewer Tutorial

Workspace Waveform Viewers
==========================

If you want to verify that your circuit is working correctly or you want to debug your circuit, it can be helpful to see what your circuit is doing in a timing diagram. You can use the `waveform viewer` to do this.

Create your vcd file
--------------------

After you've written your Verilog code (e.g., `circuit.v` or `sc2_block.v` ), you will need to create a corresponding Verilog test bench (e.g., `circuit_tb.v` or `sc2_block_tb.v` ).

Once you have run your executable, you should have a .vcd file. You may need to press the `Refresh Explorer` button after compiling to see your .vcd file.

.vcd Viewer
-----------

If you click twice on the `.vcd` file in the file navigator, it will open the waveform viewer. This viewer is currently limited to letting you view just 8 signals at a time.

If the name of the module in your test bench was `reg_writer_test`, you might see something like the following. If you click the "Add Signals" button, you will see a list of modules and signals. Notice the word `reg_writer_test` in the far-left panel (modules panel) of the viewer. The viewer shows a hierarchy of modules with each indented module being used by the module above it ( `reg_writer_test` comprises `rf` and `writer` modules). If you click on a module, the panel to the right (signals) will show the signals available to inspect in that module (e.g., `regnum` or `done` ).

You can add signals to view if you double-click a signal or you can use ctrl+click to select several signals before pressing "Add signals." After you add some signals your waveform viewer might look the following. A time cursor starts at 0s. You can move the time cursor by clicking anywhere on the timeline. If you use the magnification tools in the Zoom controls, the viewer will zoom in on the cursor. If you press the four arrows pointing out, it will expand the waveform to exactly fit the screen. If you click on a signal, you can change the radix that is used to display the signal (i.e., hexadecimal, binary, or decimal). You can also remove a selected signal by using the trash can icon. Since you can view only 8 signals at a time, you may need to remove a signal to view an extra one.

If you see an `x` in the waveform viewer, that means that the signal's value could not be determined based on the module and test bench. If you see a `z` in the waveform viewer, that means that the signal was not has not been defined by the testbench.

#### Finding Bugs with the Waveform Viewer

In this question you will be given a `.vcd` file that can be used to view a waveform generated by some Verilog code. The Verilog file was written with the goal of implementing the Boolean expression below using the sum-of-products technique. However, the Verilog file that created the `.vcd` file has a random bug in one of the product terms that you need to find. Your job in this problem will be to look at only the waveform viewer to determine which product term has the bug.

f(a,b,c,d) = a'b'c'd + a'bc'd' + a'bcd' + abcd

You may assume the Verilog code

*   calls NOT gate outputs things like `not_a`
*   uses 1 AND gate per product term
*   calls AND gate outputs things like `out_a1`
*   uses 1 OR gate to combine the outputs of all AND gates
*   outputs the OR gate to the module output `out`

In your workspace, you will need to click on the `.vcd` file to open the waveform viewer. Add some signals to the waveform viewer so that you can inspect what the circuit actually did.

Open workspace

a'bc'd'

a'bcd'

content:
You are hired by a large U.S. corporation to help them use machine learning to identify employees that are at risk of burnout due to Zoom fatigue. They want to create an application that will generate a message in the employee's calendar if they are at risk of Zoom fatigue in a particular workweek, like this:

There will be one version of the calendar message for employees at risk of moderate Zoom fatigue, and another message for employees at risk of extreme Zoom fatigue. If the employee's risk for the week is low, there will be no message at all in the calendar.

To train your model, they give you a spreadsheet of data drawn from employees' calendars and surveys of employees. The spreadsheet has the following columns

*   record index (an auto-incrementing unique ID for each row in the spreadsheet)
*   number of Zoom calls employee participated in that week
*   average duration of Zoom calls the employee participated in that week (in minutes)

*   employee experience (number of months this employee has worked at this corporation)
*   Zoom fatigue level that week (0 for not much Zoom fatigue, 1 for moderate Zoom fatigue, 2 for extreme Zoom fatigue) based on survey at the end of the week. (Note: this survey was used to collect training data, but when your model is used "in production", employees will not be surveyed about Zoom fatigue!)

#### Growth

_The below section is for extra practice, is not required, and is **not** graded._

Did you have fun, want to take this project further, or get more practice with CPSC 210 material? In software development, a project is rarely ever 'done' - there's almost always more to improve or add, and this game is no exception. See below for some extra **ungraded** activities for the lab:

*   After some playtesting, we found that players often felt confused or frustrated by the case sensitivity in the game. Can you update the game to accept a player's input as correct, even if they enter the wrong case of the expected character? (e.g. typing 'A' instead of 'a' or the other way around)
    
    *   **Difficulty:** Easy
    *   **Time:** ~10-30min
    *   **Related Concepts:** Conditional Logic
    *   **Useful References:** Character.toLowerCase(char)
    
      
    
*   Some players seem to think the game is too easy, and want to make the puppy's progress reset if you type the incorrect character. Can you update the game to require the player to type the name correctly without mistakes to call it?
    
    *   **Difficulty:** Easy
    *   **Time:** ~10-30min
    *   **Related Concepts:** Control Flow
    *   **Useful References:** Puppy's `resetProgress` method
    
      
    
*   Players seem to be frustrated by the current behaviour when there are multiple puppies that start with the same character - there does not seem to be a reliable way of knowing which puppy you'll end up selecting! Can you update the game to, when there are multiple puppies with the same character, select the puppy that is closest to the fence?
    
    *   **Difficulty:** Medium
    *   **Time:** ~15-45min
    *   **Related Concepts:** Control Flow, For-each loops, Conditional Logic
    *   **Useful References:** Puppy's `getX` method
    
      
    
*   Marketing seems to think the names we chose for the puppies are too dull and would like to see a variety of name lengths in each round. Can you figure out how puppy names are selected, change the names that are selected as well as diversify the name lengths?
    
    *   **Difficulty:** Medium
    *   **Time:** ~30-45min
    *   **Related Concepts:** Code Comprehension, Lists, File Reading
    
      
    
*   We updated the game to select the puppy closest to the fence when there are ties, but players still seem to be getting confused. Our game designer thinks that players should type freely, and only once they exactly match a puppy's name will it be called and the 'typing box' be reset. For example, if there are puppies Alpha, Alcho, and Alfred, I start by typing 'A' and all three puppies are selected. If I continue with 'l', all match and remain selected. Only once I type the third differentiating character will the individual puppy be selected. This will require significant work outside the PuppyCaller class too. Can you make these changes?
    
    *   **Difficulty:** Hard
    *   **Time:** 45min or more
    *   **Related Concepts:** Refactoring, Conditional Logic, Lists, Code Comprehension
    
      
    

If you implement any of these extras (or anything else!), please share your results with us on the discussion forum! We'd love to see what you come up with. If possible, create a short video/screencast. This will help us a lot making this lab better in the future!

Select all possible options that apply.

  

##### A note on switch statements and code coverage

In CPSC 110, you were taught to exhaustively cover all values of an enumeration when writing a `cond`. So why is it that in design A, we use the `default:` casein a switch statement to handle `HOUR_OF_DAY` instead of `case HOUR_OF_DAY:` ?

Although this is generally considered to be **bad design** (imagine if added another `WaitTimesGrouping` in the future),it is necessary in the specific context of the Jacoco code coverage tool's behaviour and of our lab to make it possible to achieve 100% code coverage.

If we were to explicitly handle both `DAY_OF_WEEK` and `HOUR_OF_DAY` in the `switch`, the Java compiler would require us to add a `default` case,which would be unreachable (and thus untestable).

In larger projects, full code coverage is often not realistic. A threshold is chosen, and new code must meet that threshold.However, because of how code coverage impacts your autograder score, any untestable code would make it impossible for you to get 100%,which wouldn't be ideal!

title: LED bargraph code
content:
You are using a 10-segment red LED bar graph. The LED bar graph is a part with 10 LEDs arranged in a single package.

The datasheet for the LED bar graph is: DC10EWA-red-kingbright.pdf

You connect your Pi to the LED bar graph, so that BCM pins 16, 12, 7, 8, 25, 24, 23, 18, 15, 14 are connected (through a series resistor) to the anodes of the LED segments, from the bottom to top of the bar graph.

You write a function `setup_pins` to configure the GPIO pins connected to your bar graph, and a function `write_bar` to make it display a "bar" with the bottom `k` bars lit.

import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
import time

GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM)

PINS \= \[16,12,7,8,25,24,23,18,15,14\]

def setup\_pins(pinList):
    for p in pinList:
        GPIO.setup(p, GPIO.OUT)
        GPIO.output(p, GPIO.LOW)

def write\_bar(pinList, k):
    for p in pinList\[:k\]:
        GPIO.output(p, GPIO.HIGH)

_Hint:_ In case you are unfamiliar with Python's slice notation, here's an example to show you how it works:

l \= \[0,1,2,3,4,5\]
l\[:2\] \# output will be \[0, 1\]
l\[2:\] \# output will be \[2, 3, 4, 5\]

When you try to test your work by running

setup\_pins(PINS)
write\_bar(PINS, 8)
time.sleep(5)
write\_bar(PINS, 4)

it seems to work on the first call to `write_bar` (the bottom 8 bars are lit). But after the second call to `write_bar`, you still see 8 bars lit, not 4 as expected.

Modify `write_bar` so that the bottom _k_ bars (and only those bars) are lit following a call to `write_bar`.

content:
This activity is a really fun way to learn how to use some of the Terminal commands you will need to know.Have fun with it, and try not to take it too seriously - you don't need to beat the whole game, just keep playing till you stop learning or stop having fun!

Much of the information in the game is beyond the scope of this course, so take what you can get out of it and use your judgement.In this course, you will only be assessed on the basic Terminal comands (discussed in lecture 1B including the options).

Objectives
----------

*   Practice with Terminal interfaces
*   Create and navigate directories
*   Create, modify, rename and delete files

Instructions
------------

Here is a text guide of the first few steps of the game:

### Setting up for the game

1.  Open a Terminal window in the Workspace.
2.  Change the directory to where this file is: `cd /path/to/this/folder`.
3.  Type `ls` into the Terminal; you will see two things: `README.md` and the `entrance` directory.
4.  Once you go into the `entrance` directory ( `cd entrance` ), the Terminal-based game will begin!

**Tip: When I say "go into the " room, I mean change directories using `cd <BLANK>`. In this game, a "room" is a "directory".**

### Starting the game

1.  Now that you have entered the dungeon `entrance`, you should type `ls` in the terminal to look around and seewhat's there.
    
2.  You will see there are two "things" in this room, there is a `scroll`, and another room called `cellar`.
    
3.  Let's read the scroll using `cat scroll`.
    

**Tip: When I say "read the scroll", I mean output the contents of the scroll file into the Terminal using `cat scroll`.**

1.  Great! The scroll told us that we can look and see what's in the room using `ls` and move in and out of roomsusing `cd <directory>`. Let's go into the cellar: `cd cellar`.
    
2.  Once we're in the `cellar`, let's have a look around: `ls`. You should see an `armoury`, a `scroll`, andsome `treasure`.
    
3.  Let's read the scroll: `cat scroll`. It should tell you about `ls -F`. Here is some more informationabout `ls -F` :
    

> Display a slash ( `/` ) immediately after each pathname that is a directory, an asterisk ('\*') after eachthat is executable, an AT sign ('@') after each symbolic link.

1.  That sounds useful, let's do an `ls -F` in the cellar to see what each of the things are. You'll noticethat the armoury is another room, the scroll is just a file, and the treasure has a "\*" at the end, so it'san executable. Cool! We don't know what to do with the executable yet, but let's try `cat treasure` to seewhat happens.
    
2.  Mm. Didn't work - okay let's move on and come back to this room later. Let's go into the `armoury` now: `cd armoury` and then `ls -F`.
    
3.  We see another scroll (and a potion, a treasure, and another room)! Let's read the scroll: `cat scroll`.
    
4.  Oooh, we have now learned how to collect `treasure`! Let's do that in the armoury and follow theinstructions to keep our treasure (using environment variables).
    

**Tip: When I say "pick up the `<BLANK>` ", I mean run the executable file using `./ <BLANK>`.**

1.  It tells us to go back and get the treasure from the cellar! Let's go and do that now with `cd ..`, pick up the treasure from the cellar, and then come back to the armoury.

title: Rolling Two Dice
content:
Probability distributions, such as the _Normal Distribution_ we saw earlier, aren't too bad if there is only one. But if you are working with a system that has multiple random variables (which is true of many systems!), then trying to find a probability distribution that covers all the random variables quickly becomes impossible.

So. **Probability is hard -- but vectorization is easy!** We can use MATLAB to pick values for each random variable individually and calculate the overall outcomes by combining them together. If we do this over and over, and we do it enough times, we can see how systems work for different ranges of input data, even if we can't figure out the math equation for the overall probabilities. Let's look at an example.

#### Example: Rolling Dice

If you roll one 6-sided die 10 times, you will get 10 different numbers that are in the range 1-6:

These rolls of the die can be represented by a vector in MATLAB:

Therefore, we can use the `randi` function to simulate rolling a die. For a 6-sided die, `imax` = 6 in the call to `randi`. Here are examples for rolling the die 10 times, 5 times, and 8 times:

Say we have two 6-sided dice and we wanted to know the probability that the sum of the two dice is greater than 7. We could figure this out using math, but this isn't a math class. Let's use simulation instead!

Here is an algorithm that we can use to solve this problem:

1.  Use `randi` to generate a row vector that represents 1,000 rolls of one die.
2.  Use `randi` to generate another row vector that represents 1,000 rolls of the other die.
3.  Add the row vectors together to get the sum of the dice for each of the 1,000 rolls.
4.  Use the "Counting Elements That Match" Common Pattern from the homework assignment on logical indexing to identify the locations of the sums that are greater than 7 and count them.
5.  Divide by 1,000 to get the percentage of sums that are greater than 7.
6.  Display the percentage - this is the probability that the sum will be greater than 7. (Note: we're displaying the percentage/probability in its decimal form here, so the values range from 0-1 instead of 0%-100%)

And here is a MATLAB script that implements this algorithm:

RollingTwoRegularDice.m

If you download the `RollingTwoRegularDice.m` script and run it in MATLAB a few times, you'll see that you get different answers for the probability that the sum will be greater than 7:

\>> RollingTwoRegularDice
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.415.
>> RollingTwoRegularDice
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.423.
>> RollingTwoRegularDice
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.431.
>> RollingTwoRegularDice
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.382.
>> RollingTwoRegularDice
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.397.

Our MATLAB script is giving us answers anywhere from 0.3820 to 0.4310. If we're looking to get the same answer to at least three significant figures, then this range of answers isn't really good enough. What do we do now??

Simulation has random processes/variables at its base; this means, by definition, that you get different answers from the randomness. Therefore, a key metric in simulation is **convergence** -- when you have simulated enough random data so that you get the same answer each time you run the simulation.

For this example of rolling the two dice, we just need to roll the dice so many times that we get the same probability each time, within a certain number of significant figures. If we increase the number of rolls to 5000 by changing the script (or creating a new version of the script, such as `RollingTwoRegularDiceMoreRolls.m` ) and re-running the script, we can see if our answer starts to _converge_ :

\>> RollingTwoRegularDiceMoreRolls
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.405.
>> RollingTwoRegularDiceMoreRolls
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.4226.
>> RollingTwoRegularDiceMoreRolls
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.4124.
>> RollingTwoRegularDiceMoreRolls
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.415.
>> RollingTwoRegularDiceMoreRolls
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.4242.
>> RollingTwoRegularDiceMoreRolls
The probability that the sum of the two dice
rolls will be greater than 7 is: 0.4048.

Now our answers have a range of 0.4050 to 0.4242. This is a **narrower range than before, so our answers are starting to converge**, yay! You would keep increasing the number of rolls until you got the same probabilities, out to whatever number of significant figures you need to have.

This tutorial, in addition to the videos for this week, will help you get more familiar with git commands, particularlybranching, and merging - things you will start encountering when you start collaboratively working in your repos.

title: Basic Statistics
content:
Modern engineering requires a significant amount of **data analysis**, both to understand and summarize what we know about a process and to somehow deal with what we do not know about a process.

**Statistics** can help us quantify what we do know about a process and provide some measures of what we do not know -- the _uncertainity_ that is a part of all engineering work.

#### Review: Min and Max

We've previously seen two basic statistical measures of data, the minimum and maximum of a dataset. Recall that MATLAB has built-in functions for finding the maximum and minimum values in a dataset: `max` and `min`. Recall, also, that if you use a compound return when calling these functions, you can get both the minimum (or maximum) value and its location in the dataset:

  

#### Mean, Median, and Mode

Three other common statistical measures of data are:

*   **mean** - the average of the dataset
*   **median** - the number that would appear in the middle if the numbers in the dataset were sorted in order
*   **mode** - the most common number in the dataset

MATLAB has built-in functions to calculate each of these statistical measures:

*   `mean`
*   `median`
*   `mode`

* * *

#### The `mean` Function

The `mean` function returns the column-by-column mean of a matrix, similar to the `sum` function from Assignment 3. For example, if we had this matrix `A` :

  

And we called `mean(A)` in MATLAB, we would get a row vector that contains the mean values of each column of `A` :

  

If you would instead like to work row-by-row and find the means of each row in your matrix, you may specify an additional argument of `2` to specify the 2nd dimension (by rows). For example:

  

**Note**

For a row vector, `mean` returns the mean of that row (rather than the mean of each column, which would be just the vector itself and wouldn't be very useful). This means that if you start with a vector, functions like `mean` will _always_ return a single result.

  

If you want to get the mean of all the elements in a matrix, you have a few choices:

*   `mean(mean(A))` - call the mean function twice in succession (means of columns, then the mean of those means)
*   `mean(A(:))` - select all the elements in A which creates a column vector; then compute the mean value of the column vector, giving you the mean value of the entire matrix
*   `mean(A, 'all')` - the 'all' option tells MATLAB to override the column-by-column default behavior and get all of the elements in A.

  

* * *

#### The `median` Function

The `median` function returns the median of a dataset, which is the value that would appear in the middle if the data were put into sorted order. If there is an even number of elements, the `median` function averages the two elements in the middle of the sorted elements. It works with arrays in the same way as the `mean` function (i.e. column-by-column, selecting dimensions, etc.).

In the following example, the vector `B` has 10 elements (an even number of elements). After the vector `B` is sorted within the `median()` function, the middle element is found. Since `B` has an even number of elements, the function takes the two elements in the middle and finds the mean of those values (in this case, the mean of the values 5 and 6 is 5.5), and returns that mean value as the median value of vector `B`.

  

**Warning!**

If you want to take the median of all elements in a matrix `M`, don't use `median(median(M))` - that's not correct because the median of the column medians is not mathematically equivalent to the median of the whole dataset. Instead, use either of the other approaches, `median(M(:))` or `median(M, 'all')`.

  
  

* * *

#### The `mode` Function

The `mode` function returns the value of the dataset that occurs most often. It works with arrays in the same way as the `mean` function (i.e. column-by-column, selecting dimensions, etc.).

In the following example, the vector `X` has three elements with the value 8. The value 8 occurs the most times, so that is the mode for this vector:

content:
The code for this lab is available in the following workspace.

Open workspace

**You must not attempt to make any changes to the workspace settings or to install any workspace extensions.**

#### Testing

Use the `PuppyCallerTest` class to design unit tests for the methods in the `PuppyCaller` class The methods are already roughly ordered from easiest to test to hardest to test. `handleInput` relies on helpers; so, it is the most complicated to test! Some tips:

When you are done, run the tests in the `PuppyCallerTest` class. Some tests may pass because stubs happen to produce the right value, but many should fail because the game is not yet functional!

#### Manual Testing / Playing the Game

Manual testing or "playtesting" is essential in video game development!Playtesting means having a human play the game. Playtesting may focus on players' experience, behaviours that emerge, frustrations, or even trying to break the game by systematically putting it into "edge cases". This process may reveal new test cases and design insightsthat update the whole design. In CPSC 210, we often go through the software development process (design, testing, development) and afterwards do only brief manually testing.During this lab, it can be helpful (and fun!) to playtest your work alongside your unit tests as your implementation progresses to see your work in action.

Play the game by pressing the 'play' button (▶️) on the top right of the workspace editor, across from the file names at the top. If you do not immediately see it when you open the workspace, wait around 45 seconds for the editor to load the project and try opening the `Main` class in the `ui` package. If you encounter issues playing the game, verify:

*   Your code compiles - otherwise, the build will close with no error message
*   You selected the window in the editor to type into it, otherwise your input won't be registered
*   You gave enough space to the window/editor to display the game, otherwise the puppies will overlap each other.

#### Implementation

Right now you can play the game, but as the puppies run across the screen, typing their names does nothing. Let's fix that! Complete the implementation of the `PuppyCaller` class. As you implement methods, more and more of your tests will pass. Try playtesting to see how your code is making the game increasingly playable!

**Note:** the rest of the game accesses the `PuppyCaller` class through the `handleInput` method. If that method is not implemented, the game remains nonfunctional. So, consider implementing it early! As you do, think about where and how the other methods might be helpful.

Once you have implemented the whole `PuppyCaller` class, you should see:

*   All your tests passing - if a test fails, the bug could be in the test or your implementation
*   Your jacoco report has full code coverage for the `PuppyCaller` class
*   The game is functional - emphasis on the fun!

This part can feel difficult, and that's ok! You're solving a challenging problem. Take your time through each method and experiment; use the game as your reference! As always, reach out to the teaching staff for help when you are stuck - we're here to help your learning!

#### Submit to AutoGrader

Ensure that your code passes the checkstyle test before submitting to the auto-grader. When you are satisfied that you have a complete solution to the problem, click the "Save & Grade" button below.

Your grade will comprise a score from running our reference tests (weighted 50%), a score based on the number of bugs identified when your tests are run against incorrect implementations (weighted 40%) and a score from code coverage (weighted 10%). The code coverage score will be determined from measures of line coverage and branch coverage.

The grader will provide hints for up to three failing reference tests. These hints may not be that helpful if you haven't already thoroughly explored your own test suite!

title: Sampling from Random Distributions
content:
Many engineering processes depend on **random variables**. A random variable is a variable that we know exists (like speed or mass), but don't know ahead of time what the value of the variable will be. We might know a range of potential values, such as with the battery example previously, or we might know some statistical measures, such as maximum, minimum, mean, mode, median, variance, and standard deviation. Not knowing the value of a variable creates uncertainty in the system, and we handle that _uncertainty_ through _probabilities_.

You may have heard of the _Normal Distribution_ or "bell-curve". A **normally-distributed** set of data is characterized, in part, by a histogram that is symmetrical about the mean of the data set. Here is an example of a histogram of normally-distributed data:

A normally-distributed set of data is fully defined by its mean and standard deviation. So, another way to create a starter set of data is to create random samples from a probability distribution.

MATLAB provides functions for sampling from a variety of probability distributions. This allows us to run simulations of random variables if we know the parameters of their distributions. For example, to simulate a uniform discrete distribution, we use the `randi` function:

In this lab, you will be working on an analysis tool that will help us find some interesting trends in emergency room wait times. In British Columbia, many emergency rooms publish wait time information every 5 minutes on edwaittimes.ca, and we collected a sample of several weeks of this data to analyse. With this data, you will create a tool that will help us explore how wait times are affected by different factors. An example of question we want to answer is "How are wait times affected by the day of the week?" where the factor is the day of the week.

We'll do this by grouping the wait times records by some factor. An example group for day of the week would be "Sunday". We will then compare the averages across all groups by producing a bar chart. So far, we are only interested in seeing how wait times differ by day of the week, but we may want to add more in the future.

#### List of Responsibilities

In terms of things we need our code to do, we can break it down into a few responsibilities:

1.  Representing all the factors that this tool can group wait times by
    *   For example: by day of week, hour of day, etc.
2.  Getting information about factors
    *   For example: finding the name/label of a factor (e.g. `"Day of week"` )
3.  Getting all the possible groups for a given factor
    *   For example, for our first factor (day of week), all the possible groups are the days of the week: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, etc.
4.  Finding the group for a given wait time record
5.  Putting a wait time record into its group
6.  Finding the average of these groups of wait times

The NAME, MNEMONIC columns tell you a descriptive name (add or add immediate) and a short mnemonic that you will use in your assembly programs ( `add` or `addi` ).

The FORMAT column tells you what basic instruction format the instruction uses for its machine code. See next section for more information on instruction formats.

The OPERATION column provides a Verilog description of what the instruction should ultimately implement. Values on the right are taken from immediately before the positive clock edge and are assigned to the value on the left immediately after the next positive clock edge. `R[ ]` refers to the contents of a register in the register file. `M[ ]` refers to the contents of a memory address in the data memory. `PC` refers to the Program Counter's contents. All other signal names are explained in the footnotes indicated by the numbers in parentheses. Reminder: Curly braces (i.e., `{ }` ) are used for concatenating wires into a bus.

The OPCODE/FUNCT column has either one or two numbers represented in 6-bit hexadecimal (i.e., 0 means 00 0000 and 20 hex  means 10 0000). If the instruction format is R, then the first number is the 6-bit opcode and the second number is the 6-bit funct code. If the instruction format is I or J, then the number is the 6-bit opcode - these instruction formats do not have a funct code.

Basic Instruction Formats
-------------------------

You will need to know only these three basic instruction formats. All MIPS instructions are encoded as 32-bit pieces of data that can be parsed into smaller fields. The names of the fields and which bits are allocated to each field are shown in the figure. One important thing to notice is that the order of fields in the instruction formats do not match the order of fields in the Verilog or MIPS assembly. For example, if you had the instruction `add $5, $3, $8`, you would be assigning your data to `R[5]`. The `add` instruction's Verilog is `R[rd]=R[rs] + R[rt]`. Consequently, `$5` is `rd`, `$3` is `rs`, and `$8` is `rt`, so that the Verilog and assembly mnemonic match.

Notes on Assembly Format Norms
------------------------------

*   `$r **s**` is a **s** ource register exclusively, `$r **d**` is a **d** estination register exclusively, `$r **t**` **t** ransitions between being a source and a destination register
*   Assignment generally goes to the left for instructions that do not use the data memory (e.g., `add $rd, $rs, $rt` is assigning to `$rd`. `lui $rt, imm` is assigning to `$rt` )
*   If multiple registers are used as sources, `$rs` is listed first, `$rt` is listed second (e.g., `or $rd, $rs, $rt` has two sources as does `beq $rs, $rt, imm` )
*   Any instruction that reads from (e.g., `lb` or `lw` ), or writes to (e.g., `sb` or `sw` ), data memory treats `R[rs]` as a base address pointer and `imm` as an offset from that base pointer. This **base+offset** behavior is indicated by the `imm($rs)` notation, where the address of the data to be read from or written to in data memory is always `R[rs]+SignExtImm`. Consequently, all data memory instructions use the `$rt, imm($rs)` format. `$rt` transitions from being a source or a destination.

Converting MIPS Assembly to Machine Code
----------------------------------------

1.  Find the MIPS assembly instruction in the Core Instruction Set table
2.  Use the second-to-last column to identify the instruction's machine code format. The format will be either R, I, or J. Use the Basic Instruction Format figures to identify the fields you need for that instruction format.
3.  If it's I-type or J-type format, use the last column to find the opcode (e.g., `andi` has opcode c hex and `jal` has opcode 3 hex ) and convert the hexadecimal opcode to 6-bit unsigned binary (e.g., e hex becomes 001110 and 23 hex becomes 100011).  If it's R-type format, use the last column to find the opcode (first number) and funct code (second number) (e.g., `jr` has opcode 0 and funct code 08 hex and `mfc0` has opcode 10 hex and funct code 0) and convert both to 6-bit unsigned binary.
4.  If it's J-type format, take the 32-bit instruction memory address signified by the label, strip off the 4 most-significant bits (they will be added back in by `PC+4[31:28]` ) and strip off the 2 least-significant bits (they will be added back in by `2'b0` ), leaving you with the 26-bit address field for the J-type instruction.
5.  If it's I-type or R-type format, use the Assembly Format column to map the fields of the assembly code to the fields of the instruction format. Convert `$rs`, `$rt`, `$rd`, and `shamt` fields into 5-bit unsigned binary (e.g., `$rs` = `$6` becomes 00110 and `shamt` = 12 becomes 01100). Convert the immediate field into 16-bit 2's complement representation (e.g., imm=24 becomes 0000 0000 0001 1000 and imm=-1 becomes 1111 1111 1111 1111). Any field that is not specified by the Assembly Format column should be all 0s (e.g., `shamt` should 00000 for `add` and `rs` should be 00000 for `lui` ).
6.  Concatenate all of the fields of your instruction format together as shown in the Basic Instruction Formats diagram. Example: `or $8, $15, $20` is an R-type instruction with opcode=000000 (0 hex ), funct code=100101 (25 hex ), `$rs` = `$15` = 01111, `$rt` = `$20` = 10100, `$rd` = `$8` = 01000, `shamt` = 00000, so the machine code would be 000000 01111 10100 01000 00000 100101.

#### Examples

`add $5, $3, $8` maps to machine code 000000   00011    01000    00101   00000   100000

`addi $5, $3, -8` maps to machine code 001000   00011    00101    1111111111111000

`j 0x0000000c` maps to machine code 000010   00000000000000000000000011

Pseudoinstructions
------------------

Instructions that you can use when writing assembly code but are not real instructions. These instructions will be converted into real instructions by the assembler. These instructions do not have opcodes or instruction formats because they cannot be translated directly into machine code.

Note: How branch pseudoinstructions get turned into real machine code can vary based on which constants or registers are used. For example, `beq $5, 4, label` would assemble to `ori $1, $0, 4       beq $1, $5, label` but `beq $5, 0xdeadbeef, label` would assemble to `lui $1, $0, 0xdead       ori $1, $1, 0xbeef       beq $1, $5, label`. Consequently, we cannot easily say how much `PC` should increment after branch pseudoinstructions. Rather than specifically indicate how much `PC` would increment, we write `PC=NextInstructionInProgram`, where `NextInstructionInProgram` is address of the instruction in your program that appears after the branch pseudoinstruction in the assembly.

These register names signal conventions (or agreed upon behaviors) that will help your code play nicely with code written by other people.

*   `$0` ( `$zero` ) is not really a register and always stores the value **0** and cannot be written to.
*   `$1` ( `$at` ) **A** ssembler **T** emporary is a special reserved register that you should never use so that your assembler can use it when it needs an extra temporary register without messing up your code. This register may be overwritten by any function you call.

*   `$16-23` ( `$s0-$s7` )  **S** aved temporary registers that you can use however you want in your code, but you must return them back to their original state before you return from your function. If everyone follows convention, then you can rest assured that these registers will always be returned with their original values after any function you call.
*   `$26-27` ( `$k0-$k1` ) Kernel temporary registers that only the Operating System can use. These registers may be overwritten by any function you call.
*   `$28` ( `$gp` ) **G** lobal  **P** ointer provides a pointer to where we store global variables in data memory. If everyone follows convention, then you can rest assured that these registers will always be returned with their original values after any function you call.

*   `$30` ( `$fp` ) **F** rame **P** ointer provides a pointer to where we store the heap in data memory. If everyone follows convention, then you can rest assured that these registers will always be returned with their original values after any function you call.
*   `$31` ( `$ra` ) **R** eturn **A** ddress provides a pointer to the instruction after the function that called our current function in instruction memory. These registers may be overwritten by any function you call.

### Conventions and Practices for Register Saving and Function Calls

**Caller Save Conventions** : Registers that are not saved across a function call (e.g., `$a0`, `$v0`, `$t0` ) by convention are considered caller-save registers. To uphold convention, the function that calls another function (the caller) must save the value of any caller-save register on the stack before a function call if the programmers wants to recover the value of those caller-save registers after the function call. The function that is called (the callee) is free to modify caller-save registers without breaking convention. The programmer must restore the value of caller-save registers from the stack after the function call when they wish to use those registers' value again.

**Callee Save Conventions** : Registers that are saved across a function call (e.g., `$s0` and `$sp` ) by convention are considered callee-save registers. The function that is called by another function (the callee) must restore callee-save registers to their original values by the end of the function call. To uphold convention, the programmer must save any callee-save registers they plan to use onto the stack before modifying them. The programmer must restore the value of those callee-save registers from the stack before returning from the function. MIPS Style Guide    

MIPS Style Guidelines
=====================

### Syntax highlighting

Syntax highlighting greatly enhances the readability of your code and helps catch simple mistakes like typing `$tO` vs `$t0`.

### Indentation

Labels should never be indented, and instructions should always be indented one tab. You should set your tab width to 3-8 spaces and prevent your editor from expanding tabs (Google is your friend if you’re not sure how to).

### Commenting

Comments are essential to understanding what your code is doing and figuring out why it might be breaking, particularly since assembly lacks such niceties as variable names, so be liberal with commenting. A helpful guideline is to make a note of which C statement (or part of a statement) each instruction corresponds to, although this isn’t always straightforward, since some statements involve a lot of intermediate steps and conditions are usually inverted.

### Instruction formatting

The first operand of every instruction should be aligned; the easiest way to do this is to set your tab width to 3-8 spaces and then tab after the instruction name. Comments should also be aligned, and once again, tabs are the best way to achieve this (although you might need more than one).

### Label names

Label names should be all lower case with underscores separating words. Try to make your label names meaningful but not excessively long; a good tip is to base label names on the C control structures they correspond to. Some label names are pretty generic, so to disambiguate, you can prefix them with an abbreviation of the function name. For example, for the function called count\_odd\_elements below, I’ve referred to the start of the for loop as coe\_for.

### Examples

Here’s some C code we’ll be translating - it counts the number of odd elements in an array.

    int count_odd_elements(int *array, int size) {
        int num_odd_elements = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < size; ++i) {
            if (array[i] & 1) {
                ++num_odd_elements;
            }
        }
        return num_odd_elements;
    }
    

This is a functional but unreadable MIPS translation. Please don’t do this.

count\_odd\_elements:
li $v0,0
li $t0,0
 
foo:
bge $t0,$a1,baz
sll $t1,$t0,2
add $t1,$a0,$t1
lw $t1,0($t1)
and $t1,$t1,1
beqz $t1,bar
add $v0,$v0,1
 
bar:
add $t0,$t0,1
j foo
 
baz:
jr $ra

This is significantly better - the alignment is off, but there are comments and label names make sense.

        li $v0, 0 \# num\_odd\_elements = 0
        li $t0, 0 \# i = 0
 
coe\_for:
        bge $t0, $a1, coe\_end \# branch if !(i < size)
        sll $t1, $t0, 2
        add $t1, $a0, $t1 \# calculate &array\[i\]
        lw $t1, 0($t1) \# load array\[i\]
        and $t1, $t1, 1 \# calculate array\[i\] & 1
        beqz $t1, coe\_for\_next \# branch if !(array\[i\] & 1)
        add $v0, $v0, 1 \# ++num\_odd\_elements
 
coe\_for\_next:
        add $t0, $t0, 1 \# ++i
        j coe\_for
 
coe\_end:
        jr $ra \# return num\_odd\_elements

The MIPS Debugger uses the SPIM simulator to run MIPS code in the browser. It exposes a user interface that allows typical debugging functionalities, such as setting breakpoints and viewing values.

* * *

#### Panels

Major functionality in the debugger are grouped into different "panels". Each panel is displayed as a box with a top header. Supported panels are listed below (some panels might not be enabled for certain questions):

##### Text Panel

This is the main panel in the debugger, where MIPS instructions in instruction memory are displayed. This is where you can find your code once it is loaded into the debugger. The debugger will load some code to initialize the simulator, so your code will appear about 10 lines down. Most questions will also load in code for setting up some sample test cases for the question. These will appear after your code.

The number within brackets to the left of each instruction is the address of the instruction. Use the `Source code` checkbox to view the original source code for the instructions and which line numbers they correspond to. You can also use the `Instruction value` checkbox to see the 32-bit value (in hex) of each instruction. At the bottom of the panel is a set of execution controls (see section below). The next instruction to be executed will be highlighted.

##### Registers Panel

This panel displays the register values. The value representation can be changed to use hexadecimal (Hex), decimal (Dec), or binary (Bin). During execution, if the register value changed, it will be highlighted.

##### Data Panel

This panel shows values currently in data memory. The values can be displayed in hexadecimal (Hex) or decimal (Dec). It organizes them into rows, where each row contains 4 words (each word is 4 bytes). The number in brackets to the left of each row is the address of the starting word in the row. To the right of the row is the string representation (if applicable) of the values.

##### Stack Panel

This panel shows values currently in the stack (another region of memory). Like the data panel, values can be shown as hexadecimal (Hex) or decimal (Dec). Values are organized in rows similar to the data panel. Unlike the data panel, the rows sit at the bottom of the panel and "grow" upwards, mimicking the behavior of a stack.

##### Output Panel

This panel displays any output produced by executing the instructions. In most cases, the printing of values to output is handled by the test cases provided by the question.

##### Logs Panel

This panel displays various debugger messages and information. Common things seen in this console log panel are messages about execution, reaching a breakpoint, etc. If your code contains syntax errors, those messages will show up here.

* * *

#### Breakpoints

Breakpoints allow you to "pause" execution, letting you more easily inspect values in registers or memory in the middle of execution. Once you're done inspecting, you can "continue" execution, which will run until the next breakpoint or until the program finishes.

You can add a breakpoint by clicking on a line of code in the text panel. This will pause execution at the selected instruction. A breakpoint's instruction line will be bolded so that it's distinguished from other lines. To remove the breakpoint, click on the line again.

* * *

#### Controls

There are several controls available for controlling the execution of instructions in the text panel.

##### Scroll Checkbox

By default, the text panel will automatically scroll the highlighted instruction into view during execution. You can disable this scrolling behavior by unchecking this option.

##### Speed Selector

This allows you to control the speed of execution. Drag the selector to the left to slow down, and drag to the right to speed up. When the speed selector is all the way to the right, it will run at max speed. If your code has bugs (e.g. an infinite loop) using max speed can heavily slow down your browser or even cause crashes, so be careful when using this speed setting.

##### Sync Code Button

This button will load your code into the debugger. It will also clear all the values, remove all the breakpoints, and re-initialize the execution state so that the debugger effectively start with a clean slate. Make sure to use this button whenever you change your code.

##### Reset Button

This button stops execution and re-initializes to a clean slate without removing breakpoints. This allows you to more easily "start over" without losing all your breakpoints. If you have edited your code, use the Sync Code button instead.

##### Play/Pause/Continue/Run Button

This button is for running your code. Depending on the state of execution, the button will say something different. When execution hasn't started, it'll be "Play". When executing, it will say "Pause". When a breakpoint is reached, it will be "Continue". And when using max speed, it will say "Run".

##### Step Button

This button lets you execute a single instruction, so you can more easily "step" through your code. This is especially useful when combined with breakpoints: set a breakpoint before some code you're unsure of, run your code up to the breakpoint, then use the step button to carefully step through the instructions that follows.

* * *

#### Views

The debugger provides different "views" that exposes a select set of functionalities.

##### Run View

This view allows you to more easily execute your code and view its output at-a-glance, by exposing a minimal set of panels and controls, and running at max speed.

##### Column View

To troubleshoot your code, use the Column View to get access to the instruction text panel, setting breakpoints, and viewing register values, among other functionalities (will vary depending on the question).

##### Full View

The Full View opens a fullscreen window within the page to provide a more immersive experience with the debugger. It provides almost all the panels and functionalities in the debugger.

Lab 5: PuppyCaller
------------------

#### Learning Goals

*   Given a specification of a moderately complex abstraction,

*   test the abstraction using jUnit
*   implement the specification

*   Use appropriate control flow operators (if, for, while, return) in Java
*   Decompose a complex specification into its key test cases

**To begin, access the lab's source code by opening the workspace in the "Testing and Implementation" question, which you can find by clicking 'Next Question' on the right.**

#### Overview

In this lab, we are working on a fun typing game "PuppyCaller" that is already in progress. In the game, a farmer is at work with the help of their puppies. Suddenly a loud truck startles the puppies, and they start running away. The farmer must call each puppy by name before they hop the fence! Players play as the farmer, and type puppies' names to call them. Specifically, the game follows this sequence:

1.  The player starts calling a puppy by typing the first letter of its name. This 'selects' the puppy.
2.  The player must type the rest of its name to call it. Any incorrect input (e.g. typing 'a' when the next letter is 'c' is ignored)
3.  Once the player has typed the last character, the puppy is now 'called' and will stop running away. This also unselects the puppy, returning back to step 1.

  

The game already has a completed console-based user interface and some other functionality, but it is missing a key element: the input handler! In a game, an input handler receives the key(s) the player presses and takes the appropriate action. This is where you come in! You finish the design of the input handler class `PuppyCaller` based on its specification. Specifically, this includes methods to:

*   Get and set the current selected puppy (useful for tests!)
*   Type the name for the current puppy - corresponding to step 2 and 3 above.
*   Find a puppy whose next character starts with an input character `c` - helpful for step 1.

These pieces come together in the `handleInput` method, which receives the input from the player's keyboard, and uses the other methods to implement the logic of the game. Take time to understand the specs of the `PuppyCaller` and the `Puppy` class before starting! In the `model` package, you **only** need to understand these two classes to complete the lab.

title: Error Bars
content:
Engineering data is often plotted with error bars included. Error bars can be used to convey a range of values for each point on the plot or uncertainty about a measured value. MATLAB's `errorbar` function will create a plot with "error bars" at each data point, like this:

Download the `SampleErrorbarPlot.m` script and run it in MATLAB to create this plot on your computer.

The `errorbar` function needs three parameters:

*   the x-axis values of the data
*   the y-axis values of the data
*   the error associated with the data

You call the `errorbar` function like this:

errorbar(x,y,err);

Error bar plots make a lot more sense when you are using real world data, though, so let's learn more about error bar plots with an example.

  

#### Example: Battery Life

Let's investigate error bar plots more with a hypothetical example:

We work for a company that produces smartphones. Our company wants to analyze battery lifetime throughout several years of use to see if we can make the following claims:

1.  Our phones have 3 hours battery life when new.
2.  After 2 years, our phones will still have 2 hours of battery life.

A battery's lifetime is defined as the length of time the battery can go before needing to be charged. A sample set of our batteries have been put through several years of simulated smartphone use. Twice per "simulated year", the lifetimes of each battery were tested, and the mean and standard deviation of the set were recorded.

We would like to visualize the degradation of battery lifetime throughout the years as well as the amount of variability in the dataset to confirm that the company can make the two claims stated above.

The videos below show how an error bar plot is an effective tool for this analysis. Download the `batteryLife.mat` and `AnalyzeBatteries.m` files to follow along.

First, let's just make the plot.

**Video Recap**

We can use `errorbar` to create an error bar plot. We looked at how to customize our plot.

  

Now, how can we interpret these results?

**Video Recap**

Using our error bar plot, we discussed whether the company could make the original two claims that they wanted to make. Based on our data analysis, these batteries are not as good as the company claimed.

  

**Note**

Putting products through simulated use to test reliability is serious business, and analyses like this example are often used in industry to drive marketing. For example, some of the first phones with foldable screens were put through tens of thousands of flips to help alleviate customer fears about the durability of the screen. Check it out:

  

##### Exercise 1

Our company has manufactured _new_ batteries that we hope will have better performance. Let's re-run our battery analysis on the _new_ battery data to see if we can make the following claims for the new batteries:

1.  Our phones have 3 hours battery life when new.
2.  After 2 years, our phones will still have 2 hours of battery life.

Follow these steps to analyze the new battery data:

*   Download the data on the new batteries: `newBatteryLife.mat`
*   Make a copy of your `AnalyzeBatteries.m` file and name it `AnalyzeNewBatteries.m`
*   Make appropriate changes to the code in `AnalyzeNewBatteries.m` to implement the following algorithm:
    1.  Clear old data and close figures
    2.  Load the MATLAB workspace variables from the `newBatteryLife.mat` file
    3.  Create an error bar plot with the new battery data
*   Customize the plot so that it looks better:
    *   Set the line width to be 3 for the graphics object (the graphics object is the error bar plot)
    *   Add the title "Battery Lifetime Performance"
    *   Add the x-axis label "Years of Use"
    *   Add the y-axis label "Full-Charge Battery Life (hours)"
    *   Use `gca` to improve the plot:
        *   font size=20

        *   y-axis limits of 0 to 5
        *   line width=2
    *   Turn the grid on

**Heads Up**

You just have to change a few things in the `AnalyzeNewBatteries.m` file. Most of the code to implement the algorithm is already there because we already wrote the code when we analyzed the original set of batteries. We're doing the same analysis, just on a different set of data, so we shouldn't have to change too much.

title: Summary
content:
This is the end of this homework assignment! Here is a summary of what we covered in this assignment:

*   **MATLAB is often used to analyze data.** We tend to follow a similar pattern each time: Read data in from a file, look for some characteristics/process the data, and plot the data to see trends, patterns, extremes, etc.
    
*   MATLAB has built-in functions for calculating common statistical measures of datasets: `mean` (average), `median`, `mode`, `var` (variance), and `std` (standard deviation).
    
*   The `histogram` function will generate a histogram of a vector of data; if you need the number of occurrences in each bin, use the `histcounts` function.
    
*   Error bars can be used to convey a range of values for each point on the plot or uncertainty about a measured value. MATLAB's `errorbar` function will create a plot with “error bars” at each data point.
    
*   **MATLAB is also used to simulate data.** When we simulate data, we also tend to follow a similar pattern each time: Convert the math equations into a computer program, create a starter set of data and use the computer program from step 1 to generate predicted data, and look for some things / process data / plot data to see trends, etc.
    
*   The `linspace` function can be used to generate equally spaced values, similar to the range operator ( `:` ), to be used as a starter set of data.
    
*   MATLAB can also generate random values to be used as a starter set of data. The `randi` function generates pseudorandom integers from a uniform discrete distribution.
    

##### Reflection Exercise

Looking at this summary of what we just covered, which topics and skills do you feel pretty comfortable with right now?
